title: Sikkim with kids or seniors from Gangtok
meta_description: Planning Sikkim with children or older parents: altitude, the under-5 North Sikkim rule, car sickness, hotel steps, easy Gangtok sights, hospitals and pacing.
summary: Sikkim works well for families and older travellers if you keep drives under five hours, spend a night in Gangtok before going high, pick hotels with lifts or few steps and remember that children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim. Gangtok's ropeway, zoo, MG Marg and monasteries suit all ages.

sections.heading: Three things that matter most
paras: We plan Sikkim trips for three generations at a time, and the same three issues decide whether everyone comes home happy: altitude, roads and stairs. Sights matter much less. A grandparent who has climbed 120 steps to a hotel room in Gangtok and a child who has been sick twice on the road to Pelling will not enjoy the view, however clear it is.

Altitude first. Gangtok is at about 1,650 m, which almost everyone handles well. Tsomgo Lake at 3,753 m, Nathu La at 4,310 m and Zero Point in North Sikkim at about 4,700 m are a different matter, and they are reached in a few hours by road. Roads second. Sikkim's roads are narrow and winding, averaging 20–25 km an hour, and a 'short' 115 km drive takes five hours. Stairs third. Gangtok is built on a ridge, and many hotels, viewpoints and monasteries involve steps.

sections.heading: Children: rules, altitude and car sickness
paras: The firm rule first: children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim's protected areas, which include Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen and Gurudongmar. Families with toddlers should plan Gangtok, Tsomgo, Pelling and Namchi instead, which are full trips in their own right. Children under 5 are also exempt from the ₹50 Sikkim tourist fee. Check current rules before you travel.

Children feel altitude like adults but cannot always say so. Watch for unusual tiredness, irritability, vomiting or refusing food above about 3,000 m, and come down if they appear. Keep high-altitude visits short, such as an hour at Tsomgo, and keep them warm: the lake is near freezing on winter mornings. Ask your paediatrician before taking infants to Tsomgo or Nathu La.

Car sickness is the most common problem on any family trip. Seat children by a window, stop every 60–90 minutes, avoid heavy breakfasts before long drives and carry the medicine your doctor recommends. A reserved car is far easier than a shared jeep with small children, because you choose when to stop.
list: Carry ID for children, needed for Tsomgo and Nathu La permits
Pack a warm jacket, cap and gloves for every child, even in May
Book family rooms or interconnecting rooms early for May and October
Keep snacks and water in the car; roadside stops can be far apart

sections.heading: Older travellers: pace, steps and health
paras: Most healthy older travellers do Sikkim comfortably, including Tsomgo, if the trip is paced well. Our rules of thumb: no more than one long drive in a row, at least one night in Gangtok before going high, a rest afternoon every two or three days and a reserved car with a driver who will stop when asked. Avoid putting Nathu La and a long transfer on consecutive days.

Talk to your doctor before the trip if you have heart or lung conditions, high blood pressure that is not well controlled or recent surgery, and ask specifically about altitudes of 3,700–4,300 m. Bring enough regular medicine for the whole trip plus a few days, in your hand luggage. At altitude, walk slowly, drink water, skip alcohol the night before a high day and go down at once if anyone has chest pain, severe breathlessness or confusion.

Stairs are the hidden difficulty. Ask every hotel how many steps lead from the road to reception and whether there is a lift. In Gangtok, branded hotels, upmarket hotels and resorts usually have lifts; many small hotels near MG Marg do not. At Ganesh Tok and Hanuman Tok, and at Nathu La, there are steep steps; the view from the car park is often enough.

sections.heading: Easy Gangtok days for every age
paras: Gangtok has more for families than its steep streets suggest. MG Marg is pedestrian, flat and lined with benches, which makes it the best evening walk in Sikkim for grandparents and toddlers alike. The Gangtok ropeway, about 1 km long with three stations between Deorali and Tashiling, gives children a cable-car ride with a view over the town.

The Himalayan Zoological Park at Bulbuley, near Ganesh Tok, keeps Himalayan animals, including red pandas, the state animal of Sikkim, in large forested enclosures along a road you can drive or walk. Banjhakri Falls, a landscaped park around a waterfall a short drive from town, named after the shaman figure of Nepali tradition, has paths and play areas. The Do Drul Chorten's prayer wheels delight children, who can turn all 108 of them, and Enchey Monastery is a short, gentle visit by car.

For a calm half day, drive to Rumtek and Lingdum across the valley. Both have spacious courtyards, and Lingdum is rarely crowded. Keep dawn viewpoints for the adults who want them, and let the rest sleep in.

sections.heading: Hospitals, insurance and practical help
paras: Gangtok has the state's main hospitals, which is one reason we base family trips here. The Sir Thutob Namgyal Memorial (STNM) Hospital is the main government hospital, and the Central Referral Hospital at Tadong is a large teaching hospital. Pharmacies are easy to find near MG Marg and Lal Market. Outside Gangtok, facilities are basic, and in North Sikkim the nearest proper hospital can be several hours away, which is worth weighing with elderly or unwell travellers.

Buy travel insurance that covers emergency evacuation, and keep a list of medicines and conditions with your documents. Tell us in advance about mobility needs, diets and medical conditions, and we will choose hotels, room floors and day plans to suit. In the monsoon, from June to September, NH10 into Sikkim can close after landslides; with older travellers or small children we build in a spare day at the end so that nobody is rushing for a flight.
Keep emergency numbers, your hotel's phone and our team's number on paper as well as on your phone, since mobile signal fades on many mountain roads.

sections.heading: Sample family plans that work
paras: These outlines are the trips we most often build for families with grandparents or small children. Each keeps drives to about five hours or less and puts a Gangtok night before any high-altitude day.

Whatever the plan, tell us the ages of everyone travelling, any medical conditions and how far each person can comfortably walk. We will match hotels, drives and day plans to the slowest walker in the group, which is the only pace that works for a family in the mountains.
list: 4 nights, all ages including under-5s: Gangtok 3 nights with Tsomgo and Rumtek, then 1 night at Namchi or Ravangla on the way down
5 nights, children over 5: Gangtok 2 nights, Lachung 2 nights, Gangtok 1 night
6 nights, seniors: Gangtok 3 nights, Pelling 2 nights, Ravangla 1 night, with rest afternoons
7 nights, three generations: Gangtok 3, Lachung 2 (if no children under 5), Pelling 2

faqs.q: Can children under 5 go to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: No. Children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim's protected areas, including Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen and Gurudongmar. Families with toddlers can plan Gangtok, Tsomgo Lake, Pelling, Ravangla and Namchi instead, which make a full and easy trip. Check current rules before you travel, as permit conditions change.

faqs.q: Is Tsomgo Lake safe for senior citizens?
faqs.a: Usually, for healthy older travellers who spend a night in Gangtok first, walk slowly and keep the visit to about an hour. The lake is at 3,753 m. Anyone with heart or lung conditions should ask their doctor first. Go down at once if there is chest pain, severe breathlessness or confusion. Skip Nathu La if unsure.

faqs.q: Is Sikkim good for a family holiday with kids?
faqs.a: Yes. Gangtok's ropeway, zoo with red pandas, monasteries and car-free MG Marg suit children, and snow at Tsomgo in winter is a highlight. Keep drives to five hours or less, carry car-sickness medicine and warm clothes, and remember the under-5 rule for North Sikkim. Family rooms sell out early in May and October.

faqs.q: How do I avoid car sickness on Sikkim roads?
faqs.a: Sit children by a window, stop every 60–90 minutes, avoid heavy or oily breakfasts before long drives and keep the car ventilated. Ask your doctor about motion-sickness medicine. A reserved car is much easier than a shared jeep, because you control the stops. Keep long transfers, such as Gangtok to Pelling, to one per two days.

faqs.q: Are Gangtok hotels suitable for elderly travellers?
faqs.a: Some are and some are not. Many small hotels near MG Marg sit on steep lanes with stairs and no lift. Branded hotels such as Lemon Tree, upmarket hotels like The Elgin Nor-Khill and the forest resorts usually have lifts or level access. Ask how many steps lead from the road and request a low floor.

faqs.q: What are the hospitals in Gangtok?
faqs.a: The main government hospital is the Sir Thutob Namgyal Memorial (STNM) Hospital, and the Central Referral Hospital at Tadong is a large teaching hospital. Pharmacies are common near MG Marg and Lal Market. Outside Gangtok, medical facilities are basic, and in North Sikkim the nearest proper hospital can be several hours away.

faqs.q: Which Gangtok sights are best for children?
faqs.a: The ropeway between Deorali and Tashiling, the Himalayan Zoological Park near Ganesh Tok with red pandas, Banjhakri Falls park, the 108 prayer wheels at the Do Drul Chorten and an evening on car-free MG Marg. In winter, a short visit to snowy Tsomgo Lake is often the trip highlight for children over about five.

faqs.q: Should seniors go to Nathu La?
faqs.a: Only if they are fit, have spent at least a night in Gangtok and have checked with their doctor. Nathu La is at 4,310 m, the climb from Gangtok takes about three hours, and the final walk to the border involves steep steps in thin air. Many older travellers enjoy Tsomgo and Baba Mandir and happily skip Nathu La.

faqs.q: How many days do families need in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Five to seven nights is right for most families: enough for Gangtok and Tsomgo plus either Lachung (children over 5) or Pelling, with rest afternoons. With grandparents, add a night so that no two long drives fall on consecutive days. In the monsoon, keep a spare day at the end for possible NH10 closures.
